vignette: The smoke hangs thick in the valley, acrid and diesel-thick. He is twenty-eight, riding in the passenger seat of an MRAP when the road fractures beneath them. The blast does not feel like sound; it feels like a wall of compressed air slamming his spine against the steel frame. Glass rains inward. A medic's voice cracks over the radio, then cuts to static. He drags his squad leader toward cover, counting breaths that come in shallow, automatic pulls. The dust settles over twisted metal and quiet bodies. He sits in the rubble for a long time, waiting for the other shoe to drop, his hands trembling. His chest tightens with a familiar, inescapable dread. He returns home to a quiet house that feels too large. The silence presses against his eardrums. He cannot sleep without the windows cracked open, needing to hear the street, needing to know nothing is closing in. He stops watching the evening news. He avoids the highway, taking circuitous backroads to the grocery store, scanning every parked car for the telltale shape of a threat. He tells his wife, Elena, that he is fine, but the words feel hollow. He jumps when the refrigerator kicks on. He drops his coffee mug when a neighbor's garage door slams. The world becomes a grid of potential dangers, and he is exhausted from reading it. Years blur into routine. He builds a career as a tax consultant, drawn to the predictable architecture of ledgers, deductions, and seasonal deadlines. The numbers offer a kind of armor. He tells himself that if he can just balance the columns, he can balance himself. But the work seeps into his sleep and his marriage. He sits at the kitchen table with spreadsheets open while Elena talks about her day. He hears her voice, but his mind is already three steps ahead, calculating the interest on a client's audit, bracing for the next discrepancy. He misses birthdays. He snaps when the house grows too loud, then retreats to the garage, staring at a blank wall for hours until the adrenaline fades. Elena leaves a trail of unanswered questions behind her. They sleep in separate rooms, the distance measured in closed doors and quiet resentment. Now, at thirty-six, he sits across from me, his posture rigid, his eyes tracking the clock on the wall. He arrives exactly on time, but his breathing is shallow. He tells me he cannot make a quarterly tax filing deadline without calling three different clients just to hear a human voice. He describes the nights when the air conditioning unit triggers a memory of the generator back home, and he wakes on the floor, heart hammering against his ribs, convinced he fails to protect everyone. He goes to the gym not to build strength, but to burn off the kinetic energy that sits coiled in his thighs. He avoids fireworks season, cancels dinner plans with friends, and tells himself it is just practicality. The numbers on his spreadsheets no longer feel like refuge. They feel like distractions from the constant hum of alertness. He wonders, out loud, if he will ever stop counting the exits.
